pois.name: Mellon Institute columns
pois.altText: Front of the Mellon Institute: a long row of tall, smooth stone columns.

prompt.text: This building has a long row of giant stone columns. How many pieces of stone make up one column?

reveal.text: None stacked. Each column is a single piece of stone.

story.text: Each of the 62 columns here is one solid piece of Indiana limestone, about 62 tons.
When the Mellon Institute opened in 1937, they were the largest monolithic columns in the world.
The building, now part of Carnegie Mellon, reaches three stories underground.

pois.name: Dippy the dinosaur
pois.address: 4400 Forbes Ave, outside the Carnegie Museum
pois.altText: A life-size dinosaur with a long curved neck, standing on a lawn beside the museum.

prompt.text: A life-size dinosaur stands outside the museum. Is it made of real bone, or something else?

reveal.text: It's a life-size fiberglass copy.

story.text: This is Dippy, a fiberglass copy of a Diplodocus installed in 1999, 100 years after Andrew Carnegie funded the dig that found the original.
The first bone, a toe, was found in Wyoming around the Fourth of July, 1899, earning it the nickname 'the star-spangled dinosaur.'
The real skeleton still stands inside, and Carnegie gave casts to museums in London, Paris, and other cities.

pois.name: “A Song to Nature” fountain
pois.altText: A stone fountain with a wide round basin and bronze figures in the center.

prompt.text: Around the rim of this fountain's basin, bronze animals spout water. What kind of animals are they?

reveal.text: Turtles. Four bronze turtles spout water into the basin.

story.text: This 1918 fountain honors Mary Schenley, who donated the land for Schenley Park.
The figures show Humanity playing a lyre to Pan, the earth god.
Its sculptor, Victor David Brenner, also designed the Lincoln penny, so you've probably carried his work in your pocket.

pois.name: Forbes Field wall
pois.altText: An old red brick wall with large white numbers painted on it.

prompt.text: This old brick wall has large numbers painted on it. What do you think they measure?

reveal.text: Distances from home plate: 457 and 436 feet.

story.text: This wall is all that's left of the outfield of Forbes Field, home of the Pittsburgh Pirates from 1909 to 1970, and of the Negro League Homestead Grays.
Bill Mazeroski's ninth-inning home run here won the 1960 World Series. Fans still gather at this wall every October 13 to relive it.
Home plate from the last game is preserved inside Posvar Hall, just across the street.

pois.name: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Cathedral
pois.altText: A pale stone church front with six tall columns, a triangular roof above, and wide steps up to the door.

prompt.text: The columns on this church's front porch each curl out into a shape at the top. What shape do you think it is?

reveal.text: Scrolls. These are Ionic columns, a style from ancient Greece.

story.text: This church was built in 1904, but not for a Greek congregation. It was the First Congregational Church.
A Greek Orthodox congregation took it over in 1923, and it's been theirs ever since.
It became a cathedral in 1955, when Pittsburgh became the seat of a Greek Orthodox diocese.

pois.standingSpot: S Dithridge St sidewalk, in front of the columned porch.

pois.name: Bellefield Hall
pois.altText: A large red brick building on a street corner, with a tall arched stone doorway at one end.

prompt.text: Words carved above this building's tall arched doorway name who it was built for. Who do you think it was?

reveal.text: The Young Men and Women's Hebrew Association.

story.text: It was dedicated in 1926 and designed by Benno Janssen, the same architect as the Mellon Institute just up the street.
Samuel Yellin, one of America's best-known ironworkers, made the lanterns at the main entrance.
Today it belongs to Pitt. Inside are a swimming pool, a gym, and a music recording studio.

pois.standingSpot: S Bellefield Ave sidewalk, across from the tall arched doorway.

pois.name: Heinz Memorial Chapel
pois.altText: A pale stone chapel with one very tall, thin, pointed spire, standing alone on a wide lawn.

prompt.text: Shields are carved into this chapel's stone walls. What do you think they stand for?

reveal.text: Schools. They're the seals of old European universities and early American colleges.

story.text: The chapel was dedicated in 1938, in memory of H. J. Heinz and his mother, Anna.
Its tallest stained glass windows are 73 feet high, among the tallest in the world.
The windows hold nearly 250,000 pieces of glass and show 391 people.

pois.standingSpot: West side of the chapel, on the path from the Cathedral of Learning lawn.
pois.notes: The main entrance is on Bellefield Ave, across from Bellefield Hall. To keep the two trigger circles apart, this point is on the chapel's west side. The seals are carved on gables, parapets and buttresses all around the outside, so they show from there too. New text, needs team review.

pois.name: Cathedral of Learning
pois.altText: The top of a very tall, pale stone tower with long, narrow pointed windows, against a blue sky.

prompt.text: This stone tower rises high above the campus. How many floors do you think it has?

reveal.text: 42. It's 535 feet tall.

story.text: It's the second-tallest university building in the world. Only Moscow State University's main tower is taller.
While it was being built, more than 97,000 schoolchildren each sent in a dime to buy a brick.
Peregrine falcons have nested on a ledge outside the 40th floor since 2002.

pois.standingSpot: Anywhere on the lawn around the tower.

pois.name: The Hiker
pois.altText: A bronze statue of a soldier in a wide-brimmed hat, holding a rifle across his body.

prompt.text: Words on the front of this statue's base name the war this soldier fought in. Which war do you think it was?

reveal.text: The War with Spain, in 1898. Today it's called the Spanish-American War.

story.text: This bronze soldier is by sculptor Allen Newman and was put up here in 1925.
Allegheny County built it to honor local soldiers and sailors who served in that war.
Newman designed the statue in 1904, more than 20 years before this one was cast.

reveal.text: It's copper. Copper turns green as it weathers.

story.text: The church was designed by Bertram Goodhue and finished in 1910.
The copper spire is 182 feet tall.
The stained glass windows are by Charles Connick, who also made the windows in Heinz Chapel.

pois.name: St. Paul Cathedral
pois.altText: The front of a pale stone cathedral with two tall square towers, a large pointed window between them, and steps up to the doors.

prompt.text: A row of arched doorways runs across the front of this cathedral. How many do you think there are?

reveal.text: Five. Three in the middle, and one at the bottom of each spire.

story.text: St. Paul Cathedral was finished in 1906. Its twin spires were inspired by Cologne Cathedral in Germany.
This is the third St. Paul Cathedral. The first two stood downtown on Grant Street.
Andrew Carnegie paid for the cathedral's first pipe organ.

pois.name: Allen Hall
pois.altText: A six-story stone building with four tall columns across the middle and a triangular roof above them.

prompt.text: A bronze plaque by the entrance honors a famous scientist. Who do you think it is?

reveal.text: Marie Curie, who received an honorary degree from Pitt in 1921.

story.text: The plaque was unveiled in 1969 by a cardinal from Poland, Karol Wojtyła, who nine years later became Pope John Paul the Second.
This was the first home of the Mellon Institute, finished in 1914. The institute later moved to the building with the giant columns, just up the street.
Its designers decided a science building didn't need women's bathrooms, so most floors still have just one bathroom, alternating men's and women's.

pois.name: Carnegie Institute and Library
pois.altText: A long, grand stone building with a row of arched windows and a columned entrance.

prompt.text: Four bronze figures sit along the Forbes Avenue front, two by the concert hall and two by the museum doors. What do they have in common?

reveal.text: Each is a giant of a different field: Shakespeare for writing, Bach for music, Michelangelo for art and Galileo for science.

story.text: One building holds two museums, a concert hall and the city's main library, all paid for by Andrew Carnegie.
Inside, the Hall of Sculpture copies the inside of the Parthenon in white marble.
The Hall of Architecture holds the largest collection of plaster casts of famous buildings in America.

prompt.text: Words are carved in stone above the three arched doors. What do they promise?

reveal.text: "Free to the people."

story.text: Andrew Carnegie paid for the building, but only if the city promised to pay to run it.
Carnegie Museum of Art opened its very first gallery inside this library, on November 5, 1895.
Today the same building also holds the natural history museum and a concert hall.

pois.name: Panther Hollow Bridge
pois.altText: A steel arch bridge with a bronze panther statue on a stone base at its corner.

prompt.text: A big bronze animal crouches on each corner of this bridge. What animal is it?

reveal.text: A panther. Four of them guard the bridge, sculpted by Giuseppe Moretti.

story.text: Only two panthers were ready for the bridge's dedication on July 4, 1897. The other two arrived late.
The steel arch rises 120 feet above the hollow below.
The bridge closed in 2024 after damage was found in its steel. It reopened in August 2026 after repairs.

prompt.text: This stone clubhouse was modeled on palaces in an Italian city. Which city do you think?

reveal.text: Venice. The architect, Benno Janssen, based it on palaces along its canals.

story.text: Fred Rogers, from Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, swam laps in the pool here every day.
The club had a pool on the third floor, basketball and squash courts, and a 16-lane bowling alley.
When ice hockey joined the Olympics in 1920, four players on the silver-medal American team came from this club's team.

story.text: The church began in 1937, when Lizzie Shaw gathered 13 children in Pittsburgh's old Chinatown, downtown.
Its Oakland services started in 1995 in the basement of First Baptist Church, a few blocks away.
It bought this building in 2005, right next door to St. Paul Cathedral.

pois.address: near S Neville St, Schenley Park

story.text: The wooden bridge here before this one was so shaky that holiday crowds panicked, sure it was collapsing.
The newspaper promised this steel arch would never tremble, "even should they be piled layer upon layer."
The bridge and the boiler plant beside it appear in Michael Chabon's first novel, The Mysteries of Pittsburgh.

story.text: It was built between 1915 and 1917 and dedicated in 1919.
It was designed by Henry Hornbostel, who also designed much of Carnegie Mellon's campus.
Carnegie Mellon bought it in 1985. Today it's Hamburg Hall, home of Heinz College.

story.text: It was built in 1903 for John P. Bindley by his brother Albion.
Bindley tried to join the whole American hardware trade into one giant company, but the government opposed it.

story.text: It was designed by architect William Halsey Wood and finished in 1898.

story.text: World Communion Sunday started here in 1933. Churches around the world now mark it on the first Sunday in October.

pois.name: Bellefield Boiler Plant
pois.address: near S Neville St, behind the Carnegie Museum
pois.altText: A brick industrial building in a wooded valley, with a very tall, thin concrete smokestack.

prompt.text: A tall concrete smokestack rises out of the hollow. What do you think this plant heats?

reveal.text: Most of Oakland. Its steam warms most of the big buildings around here, including the Cathedral of Learning.

story.text: Michael Chabon nicknamed it "the Cloud Factory" in his first novel, The Mysteries of Pittsburgh.
It was built in 1907 to heat the Carnegie Museum. The concrete stack, from 1966, is 255 feet tall.
In its coal days, it could burn a whole 70-ton railroad car of coal in a day. It stopped burning coal in 2009.

story.text: It stands for how Pitt began in 1787, when classes were said to be held in a log cabin.
This cabin dates from the 1820s or 1830s. It was bought at auction for $1,000 and moved here in 1986 for Pitt's 200th birthday.
No one knows for sure that Pitt began in a cabin. Fires in 1845 and 1849 destroyed most of its early records.

pois.name: Oakland Square Historic District
pois.altText: A row of tall brick houses with porches and bay windows facing a small tree-filled park.

prompt.text: These houses circle a small park, like the squares of London and Dublin. What do most of them have on the front?

story.text: The first 26 houses went up in 1889 and 1890. They were advertised at $6,500 each and sold within months.
The developer, Eugene O'Neill, not the famous playwright, grew up in Ireland and probably modeled the square on Dublin's.
All 67 houses from the original development are still standing, though many have been changed.

story.text: It's named for Jonas Salk, who developed the polio vaccine in a lab right here, in this building's basement.

prompt.text: Many big buildings around you resemble Greek temples or Italian palaces. Why do you think they match?

reveal.text: They were part of a 1905 plan by developer Franklin Nicola to build a grand civic center here.

story.text: His plan followed the City Beautiful movement, which favored wide boulevards, parks and stately public buildings.
It gave us Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Hall and the Pittsburgh Athletic Association. A planned Oakland town hall was never built.
The district has 154 historic buildings, including 123 homes.

pois.altText: A Gothic-style stone building with a tall arched window and red double doors.

prompt.text: On the grounds near the shrine is a stone sundial. Something important is missing from it. What?

story.text: The memorial opened in 1937, built from the same Indiana limestone as the Cathedral of Learning, by the same architect.
It honors songwriter Stephen Foster, and it holds one of his own pianos.
A stained glass window in the lobby misspells Shakespeare's name.

pois.name: Syria Mosque
pois.address: Bigelow Blvd, site now a parking lot
pois.altText: An old photo of a large hall with horseshoe arches and bands of decorative brick.

prompt.text: A grand concert hall with 3,700 seats stood here until 1991. What do you think replaced it?

reveal.text: A parking lot.

story.text: Despite its name, it was never a place of worship. It was a meeting hall and theater built by the Shriners, a fraternal club.
On January 11, 1949, a TV broadcast from here helped launch a network linking Pittsburgh with 13 other cities.
Rachmaninoff, Buddy Holly, Bob Dylan, Bob Marley and Bruce Springsteen all played here.

pois.name: Neill Log House
pois.altText: A small one-story log house of dark hewn logs on a stone foundation, with a stone chimney.

prompt.text: On the east side of this log house is a tiny window, about one foot high and two feet wide. Why do you think it's so small?

reveal.text: It was built small for defense, and it's rare now, because most log houses around here later had their windows made bigger.

story.text: It's Pittsburgh's oldest house, probably built by Robert Neal between 1779 and 1795.
In 2024, a tree-ring study dated the beam above the fireplace to 1795.
It was rebuilt log by log in 1969. A dig on the site found 19,000 objects, now at Carnegie Museum.

pois.notes: The prompt now uses the "loophole" window on the east side. The defense explanation comes from an early-1900s Craftsman magazine article quoted in the source, which put it in the dated terms of its time; the reveal keeps it neutral. ⚠ check on site that the window is visible from outside the fence. pois.name: Rodef Shalom Temple
pois.altText: A wide yellow brick building with a broad arched entrance and colorful terra cotta trim.

prompt.text: This yellow brick temple is trimmed with colorful terra cotta. A huge dome covers the main hall. What holds it up?

reveal.text: No steel at all. The 90-foot dome is made of thin interlocking tiles, a Spanish building method.

story.text: In 1909, President Taft spoke here. It's the first recorded time a sitting president spoke in a synagogue.
The congregation was founded in 1856 and is the oldest Jewish congregation in Western Pennsylvania.
Jonas Salk, who developed the polio vaccine, was a member here.

prompt.text: This glass and iron greenhouse opened in 1893. Where do you think its very first plants came from?

reveal.text: The 1893 World's Fair in Chicago.

story.text: Steel and real estate businessman Henry Phipps gave it to the city as a gift.
Its Center for Sustainable Landscapes produces all of its own energy.
In 1896, a fire across the road was so hot it melted some of the conservatory's glass.

pois.altText: Oakland's buildings above a line of treetops, with a tall Gothic stone tower on the right, under a cloudy sky.

prompt.text: This grassy slope fills up with picnics, frisbees and sleds. What do you think once stood on it?

reveal.text: A giant round electric fountain that put on light shows at night.

story.text: Mary Schenley gave the city 300 acres in 1889 to make Schenley Park, including this hill.
Ultimate frisbee players have met here every Sunday and Wednesday for years, in almost any weather.
In summer, the city shows free outdoor movies here.

pois.name: Junction Hollow
pois.altText: A deep, wooded valley with railroad tracks along the bottom, and two tall smokestacks and buildings beyond it.

prompt.text: This deep wooded valley is named after something that runs along its floor. What do you think it is?

reveal.text: A railroad. The Pittsburgh Junction Railroad laid tracks here in the 1880s.

story.text: Before that, it was called Four Mile Run Valley, after a stream four miles from the Point. The stream now runs in a pipe underground.
In the 1950s and 1960s, planners wanted to fill the whole hollow with a research complex. It was never built.
Four big bridges cross it, including the Schenley and Anderson bridges.

pois.name: Christopher Lyman Magee Memorial
pois.address: Schenley Dr, by the Carnegie Museum
pois.altText: A tall granite slab with a bronze relief of a robed woman holding a horn of fruit, above a curved stone bench.

prompt.text: At the bottom of this tall stone memorial, water once poured from a bronze animal's mouth. Which animal?

reveal.text: A lion.

story.text: It's one of the last works by sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, who died months before it was dedicated in 1908.
The bronze woman stands for Charity. Above her are Shakespeare's words: "The quality of mercy is not strained."
Saint-Gaudens planned to carve it in stone, then switched to bronze because of Pittsburgh's smoky air.

pois.name: Westinghouse Memorial
pois.altText: Three bronze panels in a semicircle beside a lily pond, with a statue of a boy facing them.

prompt.text: Small bronze animals hold up each of the picture panels here. What animal are they?

reveal.text: Turtles, a pair under each of the six panels.

story.text: More than 50,000 Westinghouse workers chipped in to pay for it.
It was first covered in gold leaf, but people scratched their names into it, so the gold was removed in 1941.
The sculptor, Daniel Chester French, also made the giant statue of Lincoln in the Lincoln Memorial.

pois.name: Niles Depot and Town Plaza
pois.altText: A long, low yellow wooden train station with a wide grey roof held up by tan columns, and a red caboose at the far end.

prompt.text: When this yellow station came back to downtown Niles in 2009, movers changed one thing about the way it sits. What do you think they changed?

reveal.text: They turned it all the way around, 180 degrees, so it faces this plaza.

story.text: Southern Pacific built this depot in 1901. It replaced an 1870 station that had its own restaurant and saloon.
In 1981 the railroad planned to tear it down. Volunteers saved it, and in 1982 it was moved to Mission Boulevard.
The town grew up around the railroad's freight terminal here, and was named after Addison C. Niles, a judge and former railroad lawyer.

pois.notes: Niles walk draft for a test in Fremont, CA, Nov 20, 2026. Merged with the Town Plaza and caboose 467: their pins were about 30 m apart, inside each other's 30 m trigger. Keep other Niles stops 60 m+ away.

pois.name: Transcontinental Railroad marker
pois.altText: A short pillar of rough grey stones with a bronze plaque on its front, in front of an old green passenger car.

prompt.text: Most people think the Transcontinental Railroad was finished with a golden spike in Utah. How long after that do you think the last link through this canyon opened?

reveal.text: About four months later, on September 6, 1869.

story.text: The golden spike was driven in Utah on May 10, 1869. But the tracks ended in Sacramento, and passengers had to finish the trip by boat.
The line through Niles Canyon finally carried trains all the way to Oakland, linking the Atlantic and the Pacific by rail.
The Niles Canyon Railway still runs heritage trains on this stretch, the best-preserved part of the original route.

pois.name: Hillside NILES sign
pois.address: near 37565 Niles Blvd, looking up at the hill
pois.altText: Giant white letters spelling NILES on a dry golden hillside under a clear blue sky.

prompt.text: Giant white letters on the hillside above town spell out its name. When the sign first went up, who do you think it was meant to help?

reveal.text: Pilots. It was a landmark for planes flying overhead, and a way to show off the town.

story.text: The letters went up about a century ago. Locals say they were covered during World War Two, so enemy pilots couldn't use them to find their way.
Today many read the sign as a wink at Hollywood. Niles was making movies while Hollywood was just getting started.
In the late 1980s, volunteers spent their Saturday mornings rebuilding the letters in reinforced concrete and white rock.

sources: Personal blog (Flora has the link): 1926, boosterism and a landmark for pilots
Facebook group Fremont & Niles California Memories, post 'NILES SIGN RE CREATED', Dec 3, 2025: local recollections (WWII cover, late-1980s volunteer rebuild)

pois.name: Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum
pois.altText: A two-storey white building with dark green trim and a row of shopfronts, with the museum's sign over the middle door.

prompt.text: Under the museum's sign hangs a second sign with the building's name from 1913. What do you think it says?

reveal.text: Edison Theater. It opened in 1913 as a nickelodeon, one of the first small neighbourhood movie theatres.

story.text: Today it's a museum that keeps silent films and the old equipment used to show them.
It's half a block from the site of Essanay Studios, where cowboy pictures and Charlie Chaplin comedies were made.
Essanay's name comes from its founders' initials, S and A: George Spoor and Gilbert Anderson, better known as the cowboy star Broncho Billy.

pois.notes: Niles walk draft for a test in Fremont, CA, Nov 20, 2026. S and A initials: Flora OK'd.

pois.name: Essanay Studio site
pois.altText: A two-storey red brick fire station on a street corner, with tan trim, a band of diamond tiles along the base and arched garage doors.

prompt.text: A plaque at this fire station marks where a film studio once stood, in what it calls America's first Hollywood. Which famous comedian do you think made movies here?

reveal.text: Charlie Chaplin. He filmed The Tramp in Niles in 1915.

story.text: In the 1910s, the Chicago film company Essanay made hundreds of Westerns here, many starring Broncho Billy, one of the first cowboy movie heroes.
Niles hardly needed a film set. It was a rough railroad town that, people say, once had a dozen or more saloons.
Essanay closed in 1918. In 2007 this downtown, with its 86 old buildings, was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

pois.notes: Niles walk draft for a test in Fremont, CA, Nov 20, 2026. Plaque at Fire Station No. 2, 37299 Niles Blvd (Flora confirmed). Also carries the storefronts stop's facts (saloons, historic district), which had no room on this block. Saloon count is from the VoiceMap tour.

pois.name: Vallejo Flour Mill
pois.altText: The roofless stone and brick walls of an old foundation behind a chain-link fence, overgrown with grass and young trees.

prompt.text: A plaque here remembers a flour mill that José de Jesús Vallejo built just up the road. Before this town was called Niles, what do you think it was named?

reveal.text: Vallejo Mills, after his mill.

story.text: Vallejo, brother of General Mariano Vallejo, built the mill on his ranch, Rancho Arroyo de la Alameda. Its stone walls still stand at the mouth of Niles Canyon.
When the railroad came through in 1869, the town grew up around the station and took the name Niles.
The stone aqueduct built to carry water to the mill still runs alongside Niles Canyon Road.

prompt.text: This small library is older than the city it stands in. Who do you think still owns it?

reveal.text: Alameda County. It opened in 1928, long before the city of Fremont was formed in 1956.

story.text: It's named in memory of a local woman, Jane R. Clouch.
Niles has had a library since 1890, when townspeople bought a collection of 145 books to lend.
Fremont was formed by joining five towns: Niles, Centerville, Irvington, Mission San Jose and Warm Springs.

prompt.text: This building on Murray Avenue has timber beams set into its walls, like an old English cottage. What do you think has been inside it for over a hundred years?

reveal.text: A movie theater: the Manor has shown films here since 1922.

story.text: It opened on May 15, 1922, with a silent film called Hail the Woman.
The Tudor look was chosen to blend in with the houses nearby, so a movie theater could pass for a manor house.
From the 1930s on, Squirrel Hill had at least three movie theaters for forty years. Today the Manor is the one that's left.

pois.name: Forbes and Murray
pois.altText: A modern library with a tall glass front on a busy street corner, with cars parked along the curb and a bus going by.

prompt.text: Two busy streets cross here, lined with bakeries, delis and shops. Locals have a nickname for this shopping strip. What do you think they call it?

reveal.text: "Upstreet", short for "up the street", because this corner is the heart of Squirrel Hill.

story.text: It took off after electric trolleys came up Forbes and Murray in 1893. The first shops on record opened around 1911.
Jewish merchants were here from the very first store listings. By the 1950s, the strip was known for its fashion shops.
And the name Squirrel Hill? It most likely comes from the many black squirrels that once lived here.

reveal.text: A synagogue: Temple Sinai, a Reform congregation founded in 1946, made the mansion its home.

story.text: It was built for John Worthington, who died in 1918, just a few years after it was finished.
The house is about 23,000 square feet. Even so, the congregation added more space over the years.
It was named a Pittsburgh historic landmark in 1976.

pois.name: Sunnyledge
pois.altText: A large red brick house with a round corner tower under a cone-shaped slate roof, a tall chimney, and a lawn sloping down to the street.

prompt.text: At one corner of this house, the wall curves out into a big round tower with a cone-shaped roof. What do you think that room was used for?

reveal.text: It was a doctor's office: Dr. James McClelland saw patients there, and they came in through their own porch.

story.text: McClelland was a homeopathic doctor to Andrew Carnegie and the Frick and Mellon families, and he founded nearby Shadyside Hospital.
Boston architects designed it in 1886, while they were also finishing a famous house in Chicago. The wooden spindles for both houses were made at the same time.
His younger daughter lived here for 94 years. Today it's a small hotel and tea room.

pois.name: Andrew Mellon Hall
pois.altText: A large red brick Tudor-style mansion with three pointed gables, tall chimneys and a carved stone doorway, behind trimmed shrubs.

prompt.text: In 1917, banker Andrew Mellon bought this mansion and more than doubled its size. One addition was rare in a home back then. What do you think it was?

reveal.text: An indoor swimming pool, 60 feet long and lined with Guastavino tile.

story.text: The house was first built for George Laughlin, of the Jones and Laughlin steel family.
Mellon also added a bowling alley, tennis courts and gardens. Around 1940, his family gave the house to the women's college that became Chatham University.
The pool closed in 2004 and is now a board room. The university president's office is in this building.

story.text: It was Andrew Mellon's estate. Parts of the grounds were designed in the 1930s by the Olmsted Brothers, the firm run by the sons of Central Park's designer.
The campus was named an arboretum in 1998.
